articles.headline: Treasury Responds to IMF Debt Warning by Auditing the IMF's Old Homework
articles.dek: A new Treasury counselor says the Fund's forecasts are 'messy' as the U.S. runs a roughly $2 trillion deficit and the 10-year yield sits at 5.19%.
articles.catch_up: IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva warned in Bangkok that strong U.S. growth alone will not make mounting federal debt sustainable, answering Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's claim that America can 'grow our way out.' David Zervos, newly appointed counselor to Bessent, replied on Thursday that the IMF's forecasting record deserves a grain of salt.
articles.why_it_matters: Higher long-term yields feed directly into mortgage rates, now around 7.5%, and into the interest bill on federal debt. How Washington answers the warnings affects borrowing costs for households and the government alike.
body: The U.S. Treasury has answered a warning from the International Monetary Fund about American debt by questioning the International Monetary Fund's forecasting. David Zervos, a former Jefferies market strategist who is now counselor to the Treasury Secretary, told CNBC by email that it is 'good to remember how messy their forecasts have been in the past.' It is a classic rebuttal: the smoke detector has gone off before when there was no fire, and has also missed some fires.

Zervos supplied a list. According to CNBC, he said the IMF's outlook in 2008 had world growth at 3% before a global contraction, that it was positive on Southeast Asia before the 1997 collapse, and that it was gloomy on Russia in 2022 when Russia barely dipped. He also cited Argentina, which was in effect back in default by 2020 after a $57 billion bailout. Translation: the referee has made bad calls, so the foul count should be disregarded.

The argument has a structure worth noticing. It attacks the messenger's record, not the arithmetic. And the arithmetic, per CNBC's analysis, is unflattering. The deficit for fiscal 2026 is headed for about $2 trillion, or 6.0 to 6.2% of GDP, based on the Congressional Budget Office's $1.993 trillion estimate. Bessent has argued for a deficit below 4% of GDP by the end of Trump's term, and CNBC's analysis says there is almost no way that happens.

Then there is the growth plan. Bessent said in Dallas last month that the country must 'grow our way out' of its debt, with AI as a key engine. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget calculates it would take a decade of 7.2% growth to balance the budget through growth alone. Second-quarter GDP was just revised up to 2.2% annualized. Translation: the plan requires growth more than three times the current pace, sustained for ten years.

Meanwhile the bond market is voting in real time. The 10-year Treasury yield is 5.19%, up 123 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point) since the end of February, when the war with Iran began and oil and diesel prices jumped. Brent crude is at $126.55. Investors also want extra pay for holding long bonds because the government keeps issuing them, while companies borrow hundreds of billions to build AI infrastructure and compete for the same money.

Households feel this through mortgages. The average 30-year rate is about 7.5%, and Redfin said pending home sales fell 4% in September, the largest monthly drop in three years. The CBO estimates that if rates run a half-point above its forecast, ten-year deficits grow by $1.9 trillion; a 1.5-point overshoot adds $6 trillion. The CBO expects the 10-year to average 4.3%, against 5.3% today.

Politics offers little relief. CNBC reports Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House in the Nov. 3 midterms, Trump has pledged $5,000 checks to adult citizens if Republicans sweep, and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries wants to reverse $1 trillion in healthcare cuts. The U.S. is not alone: France is debating its 2027 budget with borrowing costs at a near 25-year high, and global debt topped $365 trillion in the first half of the year, according to the Institute of International Finance.

CNBC's analysis does offer one calming note: expensive borrowing is not the same as a crisis, and higher yields also attract buyers. The IMF may well have been wrong before. The test now is whether the Treasury's own forecast, which is that growth will fix it, ends up in the next list of messy ones.
articles.wire_headline: U.S. Treasury dismisses IMF debt warning and 'messy' forecasting

articles.headline: IMF Lifts Growth Forecast Thanks to AI Boom, Then Lists Everything That Could Go Wrong
articles.dek: The fund now expects 3.1% global growth in 2026, while warning that the buffers holding up the world economy are 'rapidly narrowing.'
articles.catch_up: The IMF released its latest forecast at its annual meetings in Bangkok, with a Middle East war still disrupting energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz. Separately, Britain reported modest August growth ahead of a closely watched budget.
articles.why_it_matters: Growth that depends on AI spending and emergency oil reserves is growth with an expiry date, and the bill for both tends to arrive as higher borrowing costs, energy prices and taxes.
body: The International Monetary Fund has raised its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% from the 3% it projected in July, according to CNBC. That is still below last year's 3.5%. The fund kept its 2027 forecast at 3.4% and its 2026 inflation outlook at 4.7%. In other words, the news is good in the sense that a smaller bruise is good.

The credit goes mostly to artificial intelligence. The IMF said AI-related investment gave the economy a 'demand impulse,' which helped the first half of the year hold up despite the war and trade tensions. Translation: companies are spending enormous sums on chips, data centers and power plants, and spending counts as growth whether or not anyone has yet figured out what the machines will earn.

The fund appears aware of this. It called the boom 'a large, front-loaded demand shock' arriving before any broad productivity gains have materialized. It also said calm financial markets may partly reflect 'AI-related exuberance.' Translation: investors are relaxed, and the IMF would like it noted that this is not the same as being right.

The second pillar of resilience is oil. The fund now expects the Strait of Hormuz to reopen in March next year and return to its pre-war state by October. In July it had assumed mid-July and March 2027, so the reopening has been rescheduled in the way that airport departure times are rescheduled. Gulf crude exports averaged 88% of pre-conflict levels in September. Meanwhile global oil reserves are being drawn down by about 2.7 million barrels a day, close to levels that could trigger sharp price moves. Brent crude stood at $126.55 on October 14, which suggests the market has noticed.

The growth is also unevenly distributed. Thirty-two economies now account for 95% of global growth, down from 54 in April. Taiwan is forecast to grow 10.7% and South Korea 3.3% on semiconductor demand, and India 7.0%. The euro zone is expected to manage 1.1%, and the Middle East and Central Asia region to contract 0.3%, with Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar facing double-digit declines. The IMF's summary was that growth is being 'reallocated,' a word that sounds gentler than what it means for the countries on the losing end.

The fund also laid out the downside scenario. If AI productivity gains fail to show up, U.S. equities could fall 20% and global growth could end up 1.1% below baseline by 2028. The S&P 500 closed at 7,744.06 on October 15, so there is a considerable distance to fall. The IMF put the chance of global inflation above 5% in 2027 at about 35%, up from 30% in April.

Governments are not well placed to cushion any of this. The IMF said advanced-economy benchmark yields have reached multidecade highs, and that advanced-economy public debt is projected to reach 115% of GDP by 2031 from 108% in 2025. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield was 5.19% on October 14. The fund urged governments to keep household support 'temporary, targeted, and nondistortionary,' which is the fiscal equivalent of telling guests the buffet is closing, but politely.

Britain offered a small illustration. The economy grew 0.1% in August, beating the 0.1% contraction economists expected, the Office for National Statistics said, as production rose 0.8% while services were flat and construction fell 0.2%. Annual growth of 2.1% was the highest since August 2022. The pound rose 0.4%, and the 10-year gilt yield fell 9 basis points to 5.3364%. Translation: a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, and the government's borrowing cost is still over 5%.

Chancellor John Healey delivers his first budget on October 28, and analysts say weaker growth squeezes his 'fiscal headroom,' meaning the room to spend or cut taxes without upsetting bond markets. Joe Nellis of MHA warned that raising taxes risks weakening spending, while unfunded commitments could push borrowing costs higher. Deutsche Bank's Sanjay Raja noted that GDP growth hit 1.8% in eight months with 95,000 fewer jobs, if one believes the HMRC data, and asked who had said productivity growth was dead. Healey will need a better answer than that on October 28.
articles.wire_headline: IMF sees milder global slowdown as AI boom offsets war hit — warns resilience is nearing limits

articles.headline: Fed Chair Declines to Say What Fed Will Do, Calls This Progress
articles.dek: Kevin Warsh says he no longer previews rate moves, even as inflation hits 3.7% and consumers start treating high prices as permanent.
articles.catch_up: The Fed raised rates to 3.75%-4% last month, its first hike since 2023, as energy costs tied to the Iran war and AI spending push prices up. U.S. CPI has now run above 2% for roughly 65 straight months.
articles.why_it_matters: If the Fed pauses in October and hikes in December, as Goldman and futures traders expect, borrowing costs stay high while wages struggle to catch up with prices. The bigger risk is that people stop expecting inflation to end, which makes it harder to end.
body: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh declined on Friday to say whether the central bank will raise interest rates again this month. Speaking in Bangkok at the IMF-World Bank meetings, he said he does not prejudge meetings and does not believe in saying now what he might do later. Markets, which had hoped for a hint, received a thorough explanation of why they would not get one.

Warsh was blunt about the change. "It's a new chapter at the Fed [and] we're not in that business anymore," he said, referring to guiding markets in advance. Translation: forward guidance is when a central bank tells investors what it plans to do so nobody is surprised. Warsh thinks investors should read the data themselves, which is a bit like a teacher announcing that the exam date is no longer discussed in class.

Investors read the silence anyway, because that is what investors do. Goldman Sachs economists led by Jan Hatzius wrote that Warsh's remarks and other recent Fed comments suggest a pause in October, followed by a second and final hike in December. CME FedWatch put the odds of no change at the Oct. 27-28 meeting at 72.3%. So the Fed declined to guide the market, and the market guided itself to the same place.

Warsh also praised what he called a "synchronous tightening" by central banks worldwide, meaning most of them are raising rates at once. Translation: nobody gets to keep borrowing costs low while everyone else fights inflation, hence his remark that there are "no free riders." The backdrop is surging energy costs from the Iran war and the AI investment boom, with global public debt on pace to top 100% of world GDP, a level last seen after World War II. Brent crude was at $126.55 on Oct. 14, and the 10-year Treasury yield was 5.19%.

The U.S. government, CNBC reported, has insisted that growth is the best way out of its debt pile, and dismissed the IMF's warning that relying on growth alone will not work as something to take "with a grain of salt." Warsh was upbeat on AI, saying it should make economies that use it well richer, though the road may be "very bumpy" and its effect on jobs is uncertain. He offered "optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose," a phrase that is hard to put in a retirement account.

Meanwhile, the people paying the prices are not in a fireside chat. September CPI rose 3.7% from a year earlier, and CNBC calculated that annual readings have stayed above 2% for about 65 months, the longest streak of the century. The New York Fed's survey shows one-year inflation expectations rose to 3.9%, the highest in more than three years. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack warned that consumers are beginning to accept high inflation as "a fact of life."

That matters because of how inflation works. If businesses expect higher costs, they raise prices early, and if workers expect it, they demand bigger raises, which pushes costs up further. Rate hikes are the Fed's tool for breaking that loop, and they work less well once everyone has priced in the loop. Economists told CNBC the realistic goal is not lower prices, since deflation brings its own trouble, but wage growth that finally outruns inflation.

Until then, shoppers are adjusting. One Long Island lawmaker told CNBC she has cut restaurant meals and her friends have swapped bowling for nights at home. With midterms next month, the Fed's refusal to forecast itself may be the only prediction in Washington not on the ballot. Watch December, which everyone already seems to know about.
articles.wire_headline: Fed's Warsh withholds rate signal, praises recent global tightening

articles.headline: CoreWeave Slides, Taking OpenAI's Unlisted Price Tag Down With It, While Anthropic's Rises
articles.dek: Perpetual futures on a crypto exchange show OpenAI slipping under $1.5 trillion and Anthropic near $2 trillion, as the GPU landlord CoreWeave hits a one-year low.
articles.catch_up: OpenAI and Anthropic are private, so nobody can buy their shares on an exchange. Traders on the crypto platform Hyperliquid have instead built futures contracts that guess what each company is worth.
articles.why_it_matters: These contracts are tiny and informal, but they show how closely AI valuations are tied to the debt-funded data center businesses that supply the computing power. If the landlord struggles, its biggest tenants start to look a little less invincible.
body: CNBC reported that OpenAI's implied valuation fell more than 4% in 24 hours, briefly dipping under $1.5 trillion, according to perpetual futures pricing on the decentralized exchange Hyperliquid. Anthropic's contracts rose 2.4% over the same period and imply a valuation just over $2 trillion. In other words, a company that has not sold a share to the public is being repriced every few minutes by people who cannot own it.

Translation: a perpetual future is a bet that never expires. Traders go long or short, and a funding rate keeps the contract price near a reference "oracle" price. For private companies, CNBC said, that oracle estimates value from things like private funding rounds and secondary market transactions, which is to say, from the last few times anyone actually bought a piece of the company.

The market is also small. Open interest, the total of long and short positions, is more than $41 million for Anthropic and under $7 million for OpenAI, per CNBC. For scale, a valuation in the trillions is being signaled by positions that would not cover the catering budget of a mid-sized data center. The listings come from a deployer called Entropy IO, not TradeXYZ, the platform's most prominent developer, which David Schamis of Hyperliquid Strategies said typically waits for public S-1 filings.

Schamis said liquidity should deepen once TradeXYZ lists these companies, and that such contracts generally trade at a premium to the IPO price but predict post-IPO levels well. That is a reassuring claim about a product whose subjects have not yet gone public, and so cannot yet be checked.

The reason OpenAI fell more is CoreWeave, which CNBC describes as a GPU rent-a-center. Its shares touched a new one-year low on Thursday, extending a 54% decline over that period, as worries grow about how it finances itself with debt. Its OpenAI relationship dates further back and was worth at least $22 billion as of September 2025, including a five-year agreement for data centers and technology.

Anthropic is also a CoreWeave customer. The company announced in April a deal to power Claude products, though it did not disclose the value. So Anthropic has exposure to the same landlord, just with less paperwork showing how much. Both companies' contracts remain down roughly 15% from last month's highs, according to Hyperliquid pricing.

The broader backdrop is a debt story. An Investing.com roundup framed CoreWeave's stress as a test of private credit's AI financing boom, meaning the lenders who funded the building of all this computing capacity are now watching one of its borrowers. The sources do not detail the terms, so the extent of the risk is unclear.
What to watch: whether CoreWeave's debt worries spread to its lenders, and whether the two trillion-dollar valuations survive contact with an actual stock exchange.
